\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{graphicx}
\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{hyperref}

\title{Stent Graft Patency in Femoropopliteal Lesions:
A Retrospective Cohort of 212 Patients}
\author{S.~Almeida, R.~Whitfield, and T.~Nakagawa}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Endovascular therapy with stent grafts is increasingly used for
long femoropopliteal lesions, yet patency data beyond one year
remain scarce. We reviewed 212 consecutive patients treated at a
single centre between 2021 and 2024 and estimated primary
patency with Kaplan--Meier methods. The primary patency at 24
months was 68\%, and freedom from clinically driven target
lesion revascularisation was 79\%. Lesion length and chronic
total occlusion were independently associated with restenosis.
These real-world results compare favourably with published
registry data and support the selective use of stent grafts
in long lesions.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Peripheral arterial disease of the femoropopliteal segment is
the most common cause of intermittent claudication and a leading
cause of chronic limb-threatening ischaemia.
Endovascular revascularisation has largely replaced open bypass
for all but the longest lesions, but restenosis remains the
Achilles heel of the endovascular approach, particularly in
heavily calcified, occlusive disease.
Stent grafts, which line the diseased segment with a covered
endoprosthesis, promise to exclude plaque and provide a barrier
to intimal hyperplasia, at the cost of covering collateral
branches and complicating any future surgical reconstruction.
Registry data suggest acceptable mid-term patency, yet the
evidence base for lesions longer than 150 mm remains thin,
and practice patterns vary widely between centres.
The anatomical challenges of the segment are well recognised:
the superficial femoral artery is subjected to torsion, flexion,
and external compression with every step, and any implanted
device must accommodate these deformations without kinking
or fracturing over millions of gait cycles.
We therefore reviewed our institutional experience with stent
grafts in femoropopliteal lesions, focusing on patency,
reintervention, and the anatomical predictors of failure.

\section{Methods}
\subsection{Study Design and Patients}
We conducted a retrospective review of all patients who
received a stent graft for a femoropopliteal lesion between
January 2021 and December 2024 at our centre.
Patients treated for in-stent restenosis of a bare metal stent
were excluded, as were those with acute limb ischaemia.
The final cohort comprised 212 patients with 238 treated limbs.
Baseline demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, lesion
characteristics, and procedural details were abstracted from
the electronic medical record and the angiography archive.
Lesion length was measured on the diagnostic angiogram by two
observers, with disagreements resolved by consensus reading.

\subsection{Endpoints and Follow-up}
The primary endpoint was primary patency, defined as freedom
from restenosis greater than 50\% on duplex ultrasound or from
any reintervention on the treated segment.
The secondary endpoint was freedom from clinically driven
target lesion revascularisation.
Duplex surveillance was performed at one, six, twelve, and
twenty-four months, and annually thereafter.

\subsection{Statistical Analysis}
Patency was estimated with the Kaplan--Meier method, and
groups were compared with the log-rank test.
Predictors of restenosis were examined with Cox proportional
hazards regression, with lesion length modelled both as a
continuous variable and dichotomised at 200 mm.
A two-sided p value below 0.05 was considered significant.
All analyses were performed with the institutional statistical
package, and the study protocol was approved by the local
ethics committee with a waiver of individual consent.

\section{Results}
\subsection{Procedural Characteristics}
Mean lesion length was 187 mm, and 58\% of limbs presented with
chronic total occlusion.
Technical success was achieved in all but two procedures, and
there were no procedure-related deaths.
Distal embolisation occurred in six procedures and was managed
with aspiration thrombectomy in all cases.

\subsection{Patency}
The primary patency curve is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:patency}.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\IfFileExists{figures/plot.pdf}{%
  \includegraphics[width=0.75\textwidth]{figures/plot.pdf}%
}{%
  \fbox{\parbox[c][6cm][c]{0.6\textwidth}{\centering
  Kaplan--Meier curve pending\\[4pt]
  source file: \texttt{figures/plot.pdf}}}%
}
\caption{Primary patency over 24 months (Kaplan--Meier estimate
with 95\% confidence band).}
\label{fig:patency}
\end{figure}

Primary patency was 81\% at 12 months and 68\% at 24 months.
Freedom from clinically driven target lesion revascularisation
was 88\% and 79\% at the same time points.
On multivariable analysis, lesion length above 200 mm and
chronic total occlusion were independently associated with
restenosis, whereas diabetes and renal function were not.
Loss of patency clustered in the first year, after which the
curve flattened appreciably.

\section{Discussion}
In this single-centre retrospective cohort, stent grafts for
femoropopliteal lesions yielded a 24-month primary patency of
68\%, in line with the larger registries.
The early clustering of restenosis supports intensive duplex
surveillance during the first year, when reintervention can
still restore patency with relative ease.
The association between lesion length and failure mirrors the
bare metal stent literature and suggests that very long lesions
might be better served by hybrid or surgical strategies,
particularly in patients with a reasonable life expectancy.
Our analysis is limited by its retrospective design, the absence
of a comparator group, and incomplete capture of medication
adherence, all of which temper causal claims.
Nonetheless, the data provide a realistic benchmark for
contemporary practice and inform the consent process.

\section{Conclusion}
Stent grafts achieve acceptable mid-term patency in long
femoropopliteal lesions.
Lesion length and chronic occlusion identify patients at
highest risk of failure who may benefit from closer
surveillance or alternative revascularisation strategies.
Prospective comparison with drug-coated devices in this
anatomical subset remains an urgent priority.
Cost-effectiveness analyses that account for reintervention
rates are needed to define the role of stent grafts relative
to drug-coated balloons in health systems with constrained
budgets.
\end{document}
